message.content:
Produce two realistic, honest BUILD PLANS (documents only — write NO application code) for the Nxeon hosting platform at /opt/nxeon. The owner will decide from these before any build starts. Write them as `docs/PLAN-CLOUD-PHONE.md` and `docs/PLAN-WEBSITE-BUILDER.md`.

Understand the platform first so the plans fit reality: it runs on ONE Proxmox VE 9 host (OVH KS-GAME, i7-7700K, 64GB RAM, NVMe ZFS mirror + a 4TB HDD pool), provisions KVM VMs from cloud-init templates, and already has: customer/admin Next.js portals, a job worker, Stripe billing, a Mailcow mail appliance, and customer web hosting via nginx (see the SSL/web-server work, lib/registrar.ts, worker/websites.ts). Read enough of the codebase and docs/DOCUMENTATION.md to ground the plans in what exists — reuse existing systems (billing, provisioning, the worker, domain binding) rather than proposing greenfield duplicates.

PLAN 1 — CLOUD PHONE (concept reference: a cloud Android device service; some competitors skin Android to look like iOS). Be HONEST about the hard realities, do not hand-wave:
- **The iOS problem, stated plainly up front.** Real iOS cannot legally or practically be virtualised at scale — it requires Apple hardware and violates Apple's lic ensing. What competitors marketing "iPhone" actually ship is Android themed to resemble iOS, or genuine iOS only via banks of physical/Mac hardware. The plan must say which of these is realistic for Nxeon and what it would actually take, not promise "an iPhone in the cloud".
- **Android virtualisation options** — Redroid (Docker Android), Waydroid, Android-x86 in KVM, or Genymotion/anbox-style — with the tradeoffs (GPU need, density per host, ARM-app compatibility since most phones are ARM and the host is x86, boot time, isolation).
- **Streaming the screen to the browser** — scrcpy-over-WebSocket, WebRTC, or a VNC-like path — latency, input, audio.
- **The infrastructure gap.** The current single i7-7700K host almost certainly cannot run a meaningful number of cloud phones (no dedicated GPU, limited cores/RAM). State what hardware would be needed (GPU hosts, more RAM/cores, per-session isolation) and rough density/cost so the owner can decide whether to acquire it.
- **How it reuses existing systems**: billing (a new product/plan tier), provisioning (a new job type in the worker), the portal (a device view), session lifecycle.
- **Phases + an MVP**: what the smallest shippable version is (e.g. one Redroid Android session streamed to the browser, single-user, no scale), and what each later phase adds. Include real risks (ARM app compatibility, GPU cost, abuse/fraud potential of disposable cloud phones, legal exposure of the "iPhone" claim).

PLAN 2 — WEBSITE BUILDER (concept reference: a Wix-like drag-and-drop site builder on shared hosting). Nxeon already has web hosting + domain binding + SSL, so this is far more achievable than the cloud phone — lean into that:
- **Editor approach**: an open-source editor foundation (GrapesJS, Puck, Craft.js, or a block model) vs building one; templates; the block/section library; mobile-responsive editing.
- **Hosting + publish pipeline**: how an edited site becomes a live site on the EXISTING hosting/nginx layer, bound to a customer domain with SSL (reuse worker/websites.ts and the SSL sweep). Static export vs a rendered runtime.
- **Data model**: sites, pages, blocks, versions/drafts, publish state (additive to the schema).
- **How it reuses existing systems**: billing tier, the provisioning/publish worker, domain + SSL binding, the portal.
- **Phases + MVP**: smallest shippable (e.g. pick a template, edit text/images, publish to a subdomain), then custom domains, then the full block editor. Real risks (editor complexity, template quality, storage/bandwidth, support load).

For BOTH: match the honest, specific voice of docs/DOCUMENTATION.md (no marketing fluff, concrete file/system references, real tradeoffs). Give each a one-paragraph executive summary at the top, a clear MVP definition, phased milestones, an infrastructure/cost section, and a risks section. Where you're uncertain, say so — a plan that admits an unknown is worth more than one that fabricates confidence.

Do NOT write application code, change the schema, build, deploy, or commit. Only create the two docs. Do NOT run standalone scripts from a symlinked-node_modules tree. You may read anything and run read-only inspection (git log, grep, `qm list`, `pvesm status`, checking whether a GPU exists via `lspci | grep -i vga`) to ground the infrastructure section in reality — do that for the cloud-phone hardware assessment.

Report: a 2-3 sentence summary of each plan's bottom line (is it feasible, what's the MVP, what's the blocker), so the owner can decide fast.

## What Nxeon is

Nxeon is a self-hosted, Hostinger-style VPS hosting business. A visitor lands on the marketing site,
picks a plan and a term, pays, and about ninety seconds later has root on a real KVM virtual
machine — plus, from the same portal, domains, TLS, mailboxes, block storage, backups, game servers,
a web console, an AI build assistant, and a one-click lift-and-shift migration from whatever host
they are leaving.

It all runs on **one** dedicated server:

- **Hypervisor**: Proxmox VE 9 on an OVH KS-GAME (i7-7700K, 64 GB RAM). Storage is a 2×450 GB NVMe
  ZFS mirror (pool `data`, 358 G) for live VM disks and a 4 TB HDD pool (`tank`, 3.6 T) for backups.
- **Guests**: customer VMs cloned from cloud-init templates VMID 9000–9009, plus VMID **8000
  `nxeon-mail`** — the Mailcow appliance carrying every mailbox on the platform: the transactional
  sender *and* paid customer business email.
- **Web, worker and Postgres run on the Proxmox host itself**, not in a VM.

The product surface, in one view:

```
 MARKETING  app/(marketing)        CUSTOMER PORTAL  app/dashboard      ADMIN  app/admin
 ──────────────────────────        ───────────────────────────────     ──────────────────
```

Three properties to internalise before you touch anything:

- **Nothing mutates a VM from the web tier.** Every state change is a `Job` row the worker picks up.
  The web app may *read* Proxmox freely; it may not write. This is why "I clicked the button and
  nothing happened" is nearly always a worker question, not a web question.
- **One in-flight job per server, and the worker is strictly serial.** A 24-minute migration blocks
  every other customer's SSL issuance behind it. That is a real, unfixed design limit — see Known
  gaps.
- **Money is integer cents everywhere.** `balanceCents`, `priceCents`, `amountCents`. There are no
  floats in the billing path.

The hardware constraints are tight—a single i7-7700K with only about 10GB of free RAM out of 64GB, no GPU support beyond the BMC, and NVMe ZFS storage.

Realistically, this hardware can't host meaningful cloud phone instances; each Redroid container needs 1-2GB idle RAM plus GPU for smooth rendering, and software rendering through SwiftShader is too slow.

I'm looking at virtualization options—Redroid uses Docker containers with LXC-like density, sharing the host kernel via binder and ashmem kernel modules, and theoretically offers good density with GPU passthrough... scrcpy over WebSocket is the best fit since it streams H.264 video through the browser with low latency and good input handling. WebRTC would be lower latency but requires more infrastructure for media encoding, while VNC is simpler to reuse from the existing console proxy but suffers from high latency and poor touch/audio support. The MVP targets a single Redroid Android instance running x86 with ARM translation and software rendering via SwiftShader, streamed through ws-scrcpy to the browser portal. Phase 1 brings it into the product as a single-session feature behind a flag for internal use only, with the Plan tier, job types, worker handler, and portal view. Phase 2 will expand to multi-user and multi-device support.

For infrastructure, the current setup won't scale—we need a dedicated GPU host (either a server with an NVIDIA GPU or a Mac for iOS). A single consumer-grade GPU can theoretically encode dozens of H.264 streams, but Android GPU sharing across containers is constrained, so realistic density is around 5-15 phones per mid-range GPU host with 128-256GB RAM. A dedicated GPU server rental runs roughly $150-500 per month. Phase 2 also adds per-session isolation, billing, and session timeouts with snapshot/reset capabilities, while Phase 3 introduces an iOS-themed launcher option with app store handling and abuse controls.

The main risks are ARM app compatibility, Play Integrity and SafetyNet failures blocking banking and streaming apps, the GPU cost itself, and abuse vectors like OTP farming and fake accounts that could trigger carrier or platform bans and IP reputation damage. There's also legal exposure around marketing an "iPhone" option given Apple's trademark, plus the risk of Google Play bans on datacenter IPs.

Shifting to the website builder—that's much more feasible. For the editor, I'm deciding between building from scratch or adopting an existing open-source solution. GrapesJS looks promising: it's mature, framework-agnostic, supports drag-and-drop, and exports clean HTML and CSS.

Puck is another option if they want a React-based editor with a JSON data model and component blocks. For the MVP, GrapesJS makes the most sense since static HTML and CSS export aligns perfectly with the existing nginx setup. The published site would just be static files served directly.

For the hosting and publishing pipeline, I'd create a new job type that exports the site and pushes the HTML, CSS, and assets to the customer's VM via SSH, then reloads nginx. Domain binding can reuse the existing registrar and Cloudflare integration. For the MVP, static export is the way to go—it's simpler, cheaper, faster, and more secure than running a dynamic runtime. A rendered runtime with forms and a CMS backend could come later if needed.

On hosting itself, there are two paths: customers can publish to their own VPS if they already have one, or we offer a shared builder host for those without. The data model would be additive—new Site, SitePage, and SiteVersion tables to store the editor document as JSON, with a published pointer tracking the live version. The Website row handles the nginx binding when a site goes live.

We can reuse existing infrastructure: the billing tier system, the publish worker with SITE_PUBLISH and SITE_UNPUBLISH job types, domain and SSL handling through our registrar and SSL sweep logic, and the portal dashboard with a new Sites section and editor interface.

The MVP launches with template selection, inline text and image editing, publishing to a shared nxeon subdomain with automatic SSL, and static export. Phase 2 adds custom domain binding, draft and publish versioning, a media library, more templates and blocks—

plus mobile-responsive breakpoints. Phase 3 brings a full block editor, backend forms that send emails through our existing mailer, SEO controls, and analytics.

Infrastructure-wise this stays lean: the editor runs client-side in the existing Next.js portal, site data lives in Postgres, and media goes on disk or object storage. A single small VM hosts the shared builder. The main risks are editor complexity (better to adopt than build), template design quality, media storage and bandwidth costs, and support burden from non-technical users.

# Build plan — Cloud Phone

*Status: PROPOSAL. Documents only. No code, schema, or infrastructure has been built. The owner decides go/no-go from this.*

*Written 2026-07-27 to the same honesty standard as `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md`: concrete file references, real tradeoffs, and an unknown named as an unknown rather than papered over.*

---

## Executive summary

A "cloud phone" is a real Android device running in our datacenter that a customer drives from a browser tab — installing apps, tapping the screen, receiving SMS through a virtual number, all from a laptop. It is technically real and several companies sell it. **What none of them sell is a virtual *iPhone*, and neither can we** (see the next section — this is the load-bearing constraint, so it is first). The honest product is *Android in the cloud*, optionally wearing an iOS-style launcher, never marketed as an iPhone. The bigger problem for Nxeon specifically is hardware: **this platform runs on one i7-7700K with no usable GPU and roughly 10 GB of RAM free right now** (`free -h`: 62 Gi total, 51 Gi in use by the existing VMs, mail appliance, Postgres, web and worker). A cloud phone that is smooth enough to sell needs a GPU and RAM this box does not have. So the realistic path is: **a single-session engineering spike on this box to prove app compatibility and streaming latency (cheap, ~2 weeks), and then a hard decision about buying a GPU host before any customer ever sees it.** The MVP is one Android session streamed to one browser; the blocker between MVP and a *product* is a dedicated GPU host we do not own.

---

## The iOS problem, stated plainly

**We cannot offer a virtual iPhone. Nobody can, at scale, legally.**

- iOS only boots on Apple silicon, and Apple's SLA and licensing forbid running iOS or the iOS Simulator on non-Apple hardware or offering it as a hosted service to third parties. There is no legal x86/KVM iOS image, and there never will be.
- The iOS Simulator (the thing Xcode ships) is not iOS — it is a macOS process that compiles apps for the host CPU. It runs no real iOS, no real App Store, no ARM app binaries, and it still requires a Mac. It is useless as a consumer "iPhone".
- The only way to give a customer a *genuine* iPhone screen is to point remote-control software at **physical Apple hardware** — a rack of real iPhones on a USB hub, or Mac minis under MDM — one device (or a small time-slice of one) per customer. This is what the legitimate "real device cloud" vendors (device farms) do, and it is a hardware-logistics business — buying, racking, cabling, cooling, and RMA-ing phones — not a virtualization one. Capex per concurrent seat is a whole physical phone.
- **What the App Store "cloud iPhone" apps actually ship is Android** themed with an iOS-style icon grid, wallpaper, and control centre. The device underneath is Android. The "iPhone" word is marketing, and in several jurisdictions it is false-advertising and trademark exposure.

**Recommendation for Nxeon:** ship Android, and if we want the iOS *look*, ship it as an explicitly-labelled "iOS-style launcher" skin (Phase 3, optional). Never render the word "iPhone" or Apple's marks anywhere in the product or marketing. If the owner's actual goal is genuine iOS, that is a separate physical-device-farm business with its own capex model, and this plan does not cover it — say so now rather than discover it after building the Android half.

---

## Android virtualization options

All of these put an Android userland somewhere we can stream. They differ mostly in how they get the GPU, how many fit on a host, and how badly they handle the fact that **most Android apps are compiled for ARM and our host is x86-64.**

| Option | What it is | Density model | GPU story | ARM-app compatibility | Fit for Nxeon |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Redroid** | Android-in-Docker; containers share the host kernel via `binder_linux`/`ashmem` modules | Many containers per host (each idles ~1–2 GB RAM) | Host GPU via render node, or SwiftShader software rendering (CPU-bound) | x86 images run ARM apps only via an ARM-translation image (libndk/native-bridge) — slower, many apps crash or refuse | **Best fit** for a multi-tenant service; matches our container-per-customer mental model |
| **Waydroid** | Single Android LXC container bound to a Wayland compositor | Effectively one session per host | Uses host GPU through the compositor | Same ARM-on-x86 translation limits | Good for a *single* session; awkward to run many isolated tenants |
| **Android-x86 in KVM** | A full Android VM, exactly like our existing customer VMs | One heavy VM per session | Needs GPU passthrough (VFIO) for acceleration | Worst — native x86 Android breaks the most ARM-only apps | **Reuses our Proxmox provisioning** (`lib/proxmox.ts`, cloud-init templates) but poor density and worst compat |
| **Genymotion (commercial)** | Licensed x86 Android cloud images | Per-license | Bundled | Same x86 caveat | Off-the-shelf but licensed/per-seat cost; no source control |
| **Anbox** | Predecessor of Waydroid | — | — | — | Deprecated; ignore |

**The ARM tax is the single biggest technical unknown.** The Android app ecosystem is ARM-first. On an x86 host, an app either has an x86 build (some do), or it runs through a binary-translation layer (libhoudini historically, or libndk-translation on modern Redroid images), or it fails. Translation is slower and imperfect: games, DRM-video apps, and anything doing native crypto are the usual casualties. Worse, **Google Play Integrity / SafetyNet will fail** in a datacenter-virtualized, non-certified Android — so banking apps, many streaming apps, and Google Play itself may refuse to run. *We will not know the real hit rate until we measure it on a spike.* That is Phase 0's entire job.

**Streaming architecture is a separate decision:**

| Path | Latency | Input / touch | Audio | Reuse in Nxeon |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ws-scrcpy** (scrcpy server on-device, H.264 over WebSocket to a browser) | Low, good | Full multitouch, keyboard | Yes (recent scrcpy) | Closest to our existing browser-streaming (`terminal-server/`, the noVNC console proxy) |
| **WebRTC** | Lowest | Full | Yes | Best UX, most infra to build (media/TURN pipeline, GPU encode) |
| **VNC / noVNC** | High | Poor for touch/video | No audio | We already run noVNC for VM consoles — trivial to reuse, but too laggy and no audio; fine only for a throwaway demo |

**Recommendation:** ws-scrcpy for the MVP. It is the shortest path to a usable browser experience and mirrors the streaming pattern we already run for VM consoles.

---

## The infrastructure gap — measured, not guessed

I inspected this host directly. The numbers are not close.

```
CPU   Intel i7-7700K — 4 cores / 8 threads, x86-64          (lscpu)
RAM   62 Gi total · 51 Gi USED · ~10 Gi free right now       (free -h)
GPU   NONE usable. lspci shows only:
        - ASPEED Graphics Family  (the BMC/IPMI console chip — cannot render workloads)
        - Intel Integrated Sensor Hub  (not a GPU)
      The i7's iGPU is not exposed on this headless OVH build; there is no
      NVIDIA/AMD card. There is nothing to hardware-encode or GPU-render on.
Disk  vmdata (NVMe ZFS mirror): 291 G free of ~340 G  (pvesm status)
      vmdata-hdd (4 TB HDD pool): 3.6 T free
VMs   already running: 5 customer VMs + VMID 8000 nxeon-mail (6 GB)   (qm list)
```

What this means concretely:

- **No GPU → software rendering only.** SwiftShader on the i7 will render one Android screen sluggishly and is CPU-bound; it does not scale. There is no hardware H.264 encoder, so every stream is a CPU cost too.
- **~10 GB free RAM.** Each Redroid session realistically wants 2–4 GB. We could stand up *one* session for a spike, but only by borrowing headroom that today belongs to paying customers and the mail appliance. **This box cannot host a cloud-phone product without displacing existing customers.**
- **4 cores.** Android render + video encode + the app's own work is a couple of cores per session even when idle-ish. Four cores is a one-or-two-session ceiling before everything else on the box (the serial worker, Postgres, mail) starves.

**What a real product needs (rough, honest ranges — I have not benchmarked these):**

| Resource | For a viable service | Why |
|---|---|---|
| GPU | One datacenter/consumer GPU with hardware video encode (NVENC-class) | GPU-render the Android surfaces and hardware-encode the streams; without it density is ~1 |
| RAM | 128–256 GB | 2–4 GB per session plus host |
| Cores | 16–32+ | render + encode + app CPU per session |
| Density | **rough guess 5–15 sessions per mid-tier GPU host** | Unverified. GPU sharing across many Android containers is genuinely fiddly and may be lower. Treat as a hypothesis to benchmark, not a promise |
| Cost | A rented GPU server is roughly **$150–500/mo** depending on GPU; a bought one is capex in the low thousands | Order-of-magnitude only |

The owner's decision reduces to: **is cloud-phone revenue worth acquiring a second, GPU-equipped host?** Everything below assumes we prove the concept on *this* box first (cheaply, one session) and buy hardware only if the spike says the app-compatibility hit rate is acceptable.

---

## How it reuses existing systems

The good news: the platform's spine fits this without redesign. A cloud phone is "a provisioned thing with a lifecycle and a bill," and we already run exactly that shape for VMs and game servers.

- **Billing** — add a plan tier the same way `EmailPlan` (`prisma/schema.prisma:710`) and `GamePlan` (`:855`) sit alongside `Plan` (`:260`). Prices are integer cents, term-based, and flow through the existing checkout/renewal/dunning machinery untouched. No new billing engine.
- **Provisioning** — a cloud phone is a new `JobType` (e.g. `PHONE_CREATE` / `PHONE_DELETE` / `PHONE_POWER`) added to the enum (`prisma/schema.prisma:35`) and a handler registered in the `handlers` map (`worker/index.ts:944`), exactly like `WEBSITE_CREATE: websiteCreate` (`:972`). The worker's serial one-job-at-a-time loop, retry, and reaping all apply for free.
- **Session lifecycle** — model it on `Server` lifecycle (start/stop/reinstall/delete, `worker/index.ts`). A phone session is create → running → (idle-timeout / stop) → reset/delete. Reuse the status-driven pattern.
- **Streaming** — reuse the browser-streaming shape already in `terminal-server/` and the noVNC console proxy for the transport plumbing (auth token → WebSocket → browser canvas), even if the codec pipeline (ws-scrcpy) is new.
- **Portal** — a new "device" view under `app/dashboard`, using the shared `components/portal/Shell.tsx`, is the same integration surface as every other product tab.
- **The gate pattern** — copy the `ENABLE_REAL_CPANEL` / `ENABLE_REAL_SSL` discipline (`worker/websites.ts:39`, `worker/ssl.ts`): a `ENABLE_REAL_PHONE=1` flag so the code can ship to prod dormant and be turned on deliberately, with SANDBOX/staging simulating.

**The one place it does *not* fit:** the worker is **strictly serial, one in-flight job across the whole platform** (`docs/DOCUMENTATION.md`, "Architecture at a glance"). A long-lived streaming session is not a job — it is a persistent process. Cloud phones need a **session supervisor that lives outside the job queue** (like `terminal-server` does), with the job queue only used for create/destroy. This is a real architectural addition, not a reuse; call it out honestly to the owner.

---

## MVP definition

**The smallest thing that proves the concept and nothing more:** one Redroid Android session, on this box, software-rendered, streamed via ws-scrcpy to a single browser tab in the admin portal. Single user (us). No billing. No multi-tenancy. No scale. Manual start/stop. Behind `ENABLE_REAL_PHONE`, off by default.

Its only job is to answer three questions with real numbers:
1. **App compatibility** — of a fixed test list (a browser, WhatsApp, a bank app, a streaming app, a game, Google Play itself), how many actually install and run under ARM-translation on x86?
2. **Latency** — is ws-scrcpy over the real network usable for typing and scrolling?
3. **Cost per session** — how much CPU/RAM does one idle-ish session actually eat?

If those answers are bad, we stop here having spent ~2 weeks and no hardware. That is the point.

---

## Phased milestones

**Phase 0 — Spike / go-no-go (this box, ~2 weeks, no customer, no hardware spend).**
Load the Android kernel modules (`binder_linux`, `ashmem`) or confirm the OVH kernel supports them; stand up one Redroid ARM-translation container; wire ws-scrcpy; run the test-app list; measure latency and per-session cost. Deliverable: a one-page numbers report and a go/no-go. *This is the only phase I would authorise without a hardware decision.*

**Phase 1 — Single-session MVP behind a flag (only if Phase 0 passes).**
Plan tier, `PHONE_*` job types + worker handler, a session supervisor process, an admin/portal device view, the `ENABLE_REAL_PHONE` gate. Internal-only, one session, no billing wired to customers yet.

**Phase 2 — Product (requires the GPU host — the real spend).**
Acquire a GPU-equipped host. Multi-session with per-session isolation, GPU render + hardware encode, billing integration, idle timeouts, session reset/wipe, abuse controls, capacity accounting (`lib/capacity.ts` pattern). This is where it becomes sellable.

**Phase 3 — Polish / optional iOS-style skin.**
An explicitly-labelled iOS-style launcher option, app-management UX, virtual-number/SMS if in scope, snapshot/restore of a phone. Never the word "iPhone".

---

## Risks

- **ARM app compatibility (highest technical risk).** If the test-app pass rate is low, the product is a toy. Unknown until Phase 0 measures it. *Stated as an unknown deliberately.*
- **Play Integrity / SafetyNet failure.** Datacenter-virtualized Android is uncertified; banking apps, DRM video, and Google Play may refuse. Partially mitigable, never fully. Another Phase-0 finding.
- **GPU cost / hardware commitment.** The product does not exist without a second host we do not own. The whole plan is structured to defer that spend behind a cheap spike.
- **Abuse and fraud (serious, business-level).** Disposable cloud phones are a magnet for OTP/SMS farming, fake-account creation, spam, and app-store fraud. This risks our IP reputation, Google/Apple platform bans, and the same carrier/abuse blowback the platform already fights for VMs (`worker/abuse.ts`, `lib/bandwidth.ts`). Cloud phones are a higher-abuse product than a VPS — plan KYC/rate limits/monitoring *before* launch, not after.
- **Legal exposure of the "iPhone" claim.** Calling an Android skin an iPhone is trademark and false-advertising risk. Avoided entirely by the naming discipline above.
- **Google Play in a datacenter IP.** Play may flag/ban accounts signing in from datacenter ranges; per-session accounts and residential-proxy questions are their own rabbit hole (and themselves abuse-adjacent).
- **Operational load.** A persistent streaming session supervisor is new infrastructure outside the battle-tested job queue — new failure modes, new monitoring.

**Bottom line:** technically real as *Android*, never as an iPhone; the MVP is one streamed session provable cheaply on this box in ~2 weeks; the blocker to an actual product is a GPU host this platform does not have, so the decision the owner is really making is whether to buy that hardware — and the plan is built to let them decide *after* a cheap spike, not before.

# Build plan — Website Builder

*Status: PROPOSAL. Documents only. No code, schema, or infrastructure has been built. The owner decides go/no-go from this.*

*Written 2026-07-27 to the same honesty standard as `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md`: concrete file references, real tradeoffs, reuse over greenfield.*

---

## Executive summary

A Wix-style drag-and-drop site builder: a customer picks a template, edits text and images in the browser, clicks Publish, and has a live SSL site on a real domain minutes later. **Unlike the cloud phone, this needs no new hardware and no new architecture** — it lands almost entirely on machinery Nxeon already runs. We already turn edited content into a live, SSL'd, domain-bound site: that is exactly what the control panel's Websites tab does today (`worker/websites.ts`, `lib/actions-websites.ts`, the `Website` model at `prisma/schema.prisma:1145`, automatic DNS via `lib/cloudflare-point.ts`, and the certificate sweep in `worker/ssl.ts`). The builder is a new *front door* — a browser editor and a publish pipeline — bolted onto that existing back door. The right technical bet is **adopt an open-source editor and publish static files**, not build an editor or run a per-site runtime. The MVP is: pick a template, edit text/images, publish to a `*.nxeon` subdomain with auto-SSL. The main blocker is not engineering risk — it is **content and support**: templates good enough that non-technical users get a nice result, and the support load that a non-technical audience brings. The honest verdict: feasible and well-matched to the platform; the hard part is design and support, not infrastructure.

---

## Why this fits Nxeon (the thing to lean into)

Everything after "click Publish" already exists and is battle-tested in production:

- **The publish target is `/var/www/<domain>` served by nginx** — the exact layout `worker/websites.ts` already creates and manages (`nginxVhost()` generates the server block; `nginx -t` gates every reload; exit codes are genuinely checked — `worker/websites.ts:131`).
- **SSL is automatic** via `SSL_ISSUE` + the 30-minute `sslSweep` reconciliation in `worker/ssl.ts` — the same path that keeps every customer site's certificate alive today.
- **Domain binding** already works two ways: registration/DNS through `lib/registrar.ts` (name.com) and automatic A-record pointing through `lib/cloudflare-point.ts` (`proxied: false` so HTTP-01 validates — `lib/actions-websites.ts:164`).
- **Bandwidth of published sites is already metered** (`lib/bandwidth.ts`), and **the worker job model** (`JobType` enum at `prisma/schema.prisma:35`, `handlers` map at `worker/index.ts:944`) is the exact place a `SITE_PUBLISH` job belongs, right beside `WEBSITE_CREATE`.

So the builder reuses the entire hosting/SSL/domain/billing/worker stack and adds one editor and one publish job. That is why it is far more achievable than the cloud phone.

---

## Editor approach — adopt, don't build

Building a drag-and-drop editor from scratch is a multi-quarter project and a trap. Adopt a mature open-source foundation and spend our effort on templates and the publish pipeline instead.

| Foundation | Model | Output | License | Fit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **GrapesJS** | Framework-agnostic drag-drop editor with a built-in webpage preset | **Exports plain HTML + CSS** | BSD-3 | **Best fit for the MVP** — static HTML/CSS drops straight into `/var/www/<domain>`; no runtime; matches our nginx static-hosting exactly |
| **Puck** (`@measured/puck`) | React visual editor over a **JSON document**; renders React components (blocks) | JSON → rendered React (SSG or runtime) | MIT | Best if we want a structured block/JSON model and are willing to render React; cleaner data model, but adds a render step |
| **Craft.js** | A React *framework for building* page editors — you build the editor UI | Whatever you build | MIT | More control, much more work; only if the above two constrain us |
| Gutenberg-style block model | Heavy WordPress-lineage block system | — | GPL | Overkill; ignore |
| **Build our own** | — | — | — | No. Reinventing a solved, hard problem |

**Recommendation:** **GrapesJS for the MVP** because its HTML/CSS export lands with zero runtime on the hosting we already run. Keep **Puck** as the option if, in Phase 3, we want a richer structured block model and are ready to introduce a render step. The block/section library and templates are *our* work either way — that is where the product's quality lives.

**Templates and blocks.** A starter set of professionally-designed templates (landing page, restaurant, portfolio, small-business, one-pager) and a block/section library (hero, features, gallery, pricing, contact, footer). This is design labour, not engineering, and it is ongoing. **Mobile-responsive editing** (desktop/tablet/mobile breakpoint switching) is table stakes — GrapesJS and Puck both support device breakpoints; the responsibility is authoring templates that actually hold up at each width.

---

## Hosting + publish pipeline

**Static export, not a rendered runtime.** The MVP publishes a static bundle (HTML/CSS/JS/assets) into a docRoot served by nginx. No per-site process, no runtime to crash, no per-tenant memory cost, minimal attack surface, and it slots into the existing hosting with no changes to how sites are served. A rendered/dynamic runtime (server-side CMS, live forms backend) is a deliberate later phase, not the starting point.

**The pipeline, reusing what exists:**

```
Editor (browser, in app/dashboard)
      │  save  → Site/SitePage JSON in Postgres (draft)
      ▼
[ Publish ] → enqueue Job  SITE_PUBLISH        ← new JobType, beside WEBSITE_CREATE
      ▼
worker/site-publish.ts (new, modelled on worker/websites.ts)
      │  1. render the site JSON → static HTML/CSS/assets
      │  2. write the bundle into /var/www/<domain> over SSH/SFTP
      │        (reuse lib/ssh-exec.ts + lib/sftp.ts — same helpers websites.ts uses)
      │  3. ensure the nginx vhost exists (reuse nginxVhost() / WEBSITE_CREATE)
      │  4. reload nginx  (nginx -t gate, exactly as today)
      ▼
worker/ssl.ts  →  SSL_ISSUE + sslSweep  (unchanged, automatic cert)
lib/cloudflare-point.ts / lib/registrar.ts  →  domain bound (unchanged)
```

**Two hosting destinations, phased:**

1. **Shared "builder" host (MVP).** Customers who don't own a VPS publish to a `*.nxeon` subdomain on a single shared builder VM. This is one small VM (well within our ~291 G NVMe free per `pvesm status`) and gives a zero-friction "publish in one click" first experience. A `Website` row per published site binds it to nginx; SSL is automatic on the subdomain.
2. **Customer's own VPS + custom domain (Phase 2).** Publish straight into a `Website`/docRoot on the customer's existing server — the builder becomes another producer of the same `Website` rows the control panel already manages, on their own domain with their own cert.

**Publish must be atomic.** Write the new bundle to a temp dir and swap the docRoot symlink (or rsync-with-delete into a staging path then move), so a failed publish never leaves a half-written live site. `worker/websites.ts` already checks exit codes and gates on `nginx -t`; the publish job must add the same rigour to the file write. Call this out to whoever builds it — it is the one genuinely fiddly bit.

---

## Data model (additive only)

New models, none touching existing tables — same additive style as `EmailPlan`/`GamePlan` sitting beside `Plan`:

| Model | Purpose | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `Site` | One website a customer is building | `userId`, `name`, optional `websiteId` (the `Website` row it publishes into once live), publish state |
| `SitePage` | A page within a site | `siteId`, `path` (`/`, `/about`), `title`, SEO fields |
| `SiteVersion` | An immutable snapshot of the editor document | `siteId`, `document` (JSON — the GrapesJS/Puck doc), `createdAt`; a `draft` pointer and a `publishedVersionId` pointer give drafts + rollback for free |
| `SiteAsset` | Uploaded media (images) | `siteId`, storage path/URL, size — feeds storage/bandwidth accounting |

Publish state lives as `Site.status` (`DRAFT` / `PUBLISHING` / `PUBLISHED` / `FAILED`) mirroring the string-status convention the `Website` model already uses (`prisma/schema.prisma:1145`). Reuse the existing `Website` row for the actual nginx/SSL binding rather than duplicating that concern — a `Site` *publishes into* a `Website`.

---

## How it reuses existing systems

- **Billing** — a builder plan tier / entitlement, priced in integer cents through the existing checkout, renewal, and dunning machinery (same pattern as `EmailPlan`, `prisma/schema.prisma:710`). No new billing code. Could also be a feature flag on existing hosting plans.
- **Provisioning / publish worker** — `SITE_PUBLISH` (+ `SITE_UNPUBLISH`) added to `JobType` (`prisma/schema.prisma:35`) and the `handlers` map (`worker/index.ts:944`), beside `WEBSITE_CREATE`. Serial worker, retries, reaping — all free.
- **Domain + SSL binding** — `lib/registrar.ts`, `lib/cloudflare-point.ts`, and `worker/ssl.ts`'s `SSL_ISSUE`/`sslSweep`, entirely unchanged.
- **Hosting layer** — `worker/websites.ts`'s `nginxVhost()`, the `/var/www/<domain>` convention, and `lib/ssh-exec.ts` / `lib/sftp.ts` for the file write.
- **Portal** — a new "Sites" section under `app/dashboard` using `components/portal/Shell.tsx`; the editor is client-side JS hosted inside the existing Next.js app. No new service.
- **The gate pattern** — an `ENABLE_REAL_PUBLISH`-style flag mirroring `ENABLE_REAL_CPANEL` (`worker/websites.ts:39`), so it ships to prod dormant and SANDBOX/staging simulate the publish.

---

## MVP definition

**Pick a template → edit text and images inline → publish to a `*.nxeon` subdomain with automatic SSL.** One shared builder host, a handful of templates, a limited block set, static export, drafts saved in Postgres. No custom domains yet, no forms backend, no e-commerce. This is genuinely shippable on current hardware and reuses the entire publish/SSL/domain stack.

---

## Phased milestones

**Phase 1 — MVP.** GrapesJS embedded in `app/dashboard`; `Site`/`SitePage`/`SiteVersion` models; `SITE_PUBLISH` job → static bundle → shared builder host → auto-SSL subdomain; 3–5 templates; core block library; mobile breakpoints; drafts. Behind the publish gate flag.

**Phase 2 — Custom domains + versioning polish.** Publish into the customer's own VPS `Website`/docRoot on their own domain (reuse `lib/registrar.ts` + `worker/ssl.ts`); draft/publish/rollback UX on `SiteVersion`; a media/asset library with storage accounting; more templates and blocks; SEO fields per page.

**Phase 3 — Full editor + dynamic bits.** Richer block editor (possibly the Puck/JSON model); **contact forms wired to the existing mailer** (`lib/mailer.ts` — form submission → email, no new infra); analytics; optional structured content. A rendered runtime only if a real feature (e.g. a CMS collection) demands it.

---

## Infrastructure and cost

**Low, and mostly already paid for.** The editor is client-side JS inside the existing Next.js portal — no new service, no GPU, no new host. Costs to watch, none alarming:

- **Storage** — site JSON in Postgres is tiny; uploaded media is the real consumer. Put media on the NVMe pool (291 G free, `pvesm status`) for the builder host, or the 4 TB HDD pool for cold assets; add a per-plan storage quota via `SiteAsset` accounting.
- **Bandwidth** — published static sites are served from nginx and already metered by `lib/bandwidth.ts`. Static sites are cheap to serve; a viral customer site is the only spike risk, bounded by plan limits.
- **Shared builder host** — one small VM, trivially within current headroom.

The one platform constraint to remember: **the worker is strictly serial** (`docs/DOCUMENTATION.md`, "Architecture at a glance"). A publish is a short job, so this is fine — but a slow publish still queues behind a 24-minute migration like everything else. Keep the publish job fast (render + rsync, seconds) so it never becomes the thing blocking the queue.

---

## Risks

- **Template and design quality (highest risk, and it's not engineering).** A builder is only as good as its templates. Bad templates = bad customer sites = the product looks cheap. This is ongoing design labour, easy to under-resource.
- **Support load.** Non-technical users are a different, heavier support population than the VPS audience. "Why is my site not showing up," DNS confusion, "how do I change the font." Budget for it; it is the quiet cost that sinks site-builder products.
- **Editor complexity underestimated.** Even adopting GrapesJS/Puck, wiring templates, blocks, responsive breakpoints, media upload, and a clean save/publish loop is real work. Adopting (not building) the editor is the single biggest de-risking choice — hold that line.
- **Publish atomicity.** A half-written docRoot is a broken live site. Temp-write-and-swap, exit-code checks, and the `nginx -t` gate must all be honoured, as `worker/websites.ts` already does for vhosts.
- **Storage / bandwidth creep.** Media libraries grow; enforce quotas early via `SiteAsset` rather than retrofitting them after disks fill.
- **Generated-markup SEO/performance.** Drag-drop tools can emit bloated HTML; template hygiene and a Lighthouse pass matter if customers care about ranking.
- **Lock-in / export expectations.** Customers may expect to export or self-host their site; decide the policy up front (static export is easy to offer given we already produce static bundles).

**Bottom line:** feasible and unusually well-matched to Nxeon — the entire post-Publish stack (nginx hosting, auto-SSL, domain binding, billing, the job worker) already exists and is proven, so the build is essentially "embed an open-source editor + add one `SITE_PUBLISH` job + write templates." The MVP is template → edit → publish to a `*.nxeon` subdomain with auto-SSL, shippable on current hardware. The blocker isn't infrastructure — it's sustained investment in **template quality and the support load** of a non-technical audience.
